title: Keeping learning: classical guitar, twelve-tone writing, the Schillinger system
summary: Collins studies classics and twelve-tone scales so he knows what is happening, and says staying involved bridges the generational gap.

blocks.x: You undoubtedly know what is happening with you; you listen to the rock bands, and so on...
but what is happening with you?

Well, I'll tell you. Well, now as I told you I am really at the classics, you know. I love classical guitar, so I play classics, so I'm analyzing this. I'm enjoying it, I'm increasing my musical knowledge, my repertoire, my techniques; for the last two years I've been studying the 12 tone scale, you know, writing. You've got to be involved to see what is what and what makes everything move in certain directions. I can't let anything go by and I not know what is happening.

When the Shillinger system came out I studied the Shillinger system to see what it is. I found out what they were doing I'd been doing any way, so you know, they did it mathematically and I did it mathematically and instinctively too. You know. So this is how you stay young, this is how you analyze, this is how your playing just grows, you know.

And then found mathematically this is a -- yeah. But I did it instinctively because I could hear these things, you know. But actually you've got to be involved. You can't be stagnant if you do retire you know, shame on you. You know, I'm not going to go on pension, you know, I'm going to be involved. And by being involved I'm involved in writing, and I'm involved in playing and I just wish there were more hours in the day. So this is how you bridge the gap. There's no gap in --
